text_original: Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer (Long Range AWD) cites 0-60 mph in 4.2 s and compares its pace with a BMW i4 M50. Reviewer finds the ride brittle over sharp bumps and less composed than a BMW i4 or Polestar 2. Reviewer finds the steering hyperactive, artificial and twitchy at speed, with little feel. Reviewer calls the 341-mile EPA range of the Long Range AWD the best in its class at the price, and averaged over 3 mi/kWh. Reviewer calls Supercharging the easiest public charging experience (plug in and walk away), with up to 250 kW, but notes rivals are gaining Supercharger access. Reviewer calls the user interface the worst he has used, with small look-alike icons and menus that are hard to use while driving. Reviewer notes the rear touchscreen impresses children in the back seat. Reviewer reports the touchscreen gear-selector slider failed to register several times in under two days, and the backup drive buttons in the headliner beep loudly when pressed by accident. Reviewer criticizes the lack of stalks or physical controls for the wipers, mirror adjustment and steering-column adjustment. Reviewer states FSD handles lane keeping, stopping at red lights and following traffic well, and explains its maneuvers. Reviewer reports FSD ($8,000) twice missed a lane split, fought steering corrections and disengaged after them, and rates GM Super Cruise as superior. Reviewer finds the cabin cheap and underequipped for the price. Reviewer reports a sharp edge on the rear door that cut him. Reviewer describes the standard seats as miserable. Reviewer notes significant wind and tire noise at highway speed despite double-pane windows. Reviewer finds the rear LATCH child-seat anchors difficult to hook onto. Reviewer notes that heated seats, the large touchscreen and a rear screen are standard and that the car qualified for the full $7,500 federal tax credit. Reviewer states the interior does not justify the price, that range and charging are its only remaining advantages, and recommends the Hyundai Ioniq 6 instead. Reviewer states the BMW i4 has a nicer interior and is the better sports sedan, though dual-motor versions start above $60,000. Original excerpt(s), from tool summaries: «No Longer a Trailblazer»

Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer states the Plaid (1,020 hp, est. 0-60 mph in 1.99 s) is in a different class for straight-line speed from gasoline rivals such as the BMW M5 and Mercedes-AMG E63 S. Reviewer states the car cornered and rode exceptionally well and stayed flat through corners. Reviewer finds the steering a little heavy, though it returns to center well. Reviewer finds the yoke (then mandatory on the Plaid) awkward in multi-point turns, tight parking and long ramps, and judges it worse than a regular steering wheel. Reviewer finds the capacitive turn-signal buttons on the yoke unclear to use and easy to trigger accidentally. Reviewer found the on-screen, sensor-assisted gear selection unintuitive at first but got used to it quickly. Reviewer finds the 17-inch touchscreen better integrated into the dash than in the Model 3. Reviewer finds the flat, square displays less appealing than the Porsche Taycan's curved display layout. Reviewer reports Autopilot would not engage for him despite repeated attempts and a reset; it worked for the co-driver on the highway, with hands-on-wheel warnings. Reviewer notes the real wood trim is nicely mounted around the cabin. Reviewer finds the interior a little plain and worries that minimalism and cost-cutting, such as hidden air vents, come at the expense of function. Reviewer notes plenty of passenger space, especially in the back seats. Reviewer describes the cabin as serenely quiet. Reviewer calls the Plaid's $131,190 starting price eyebrow-raising, while noting few rivals can match it.

Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer finds the single-motor RWD (362 hp) has plenty of punch, at just over 5 s to 60 mph. Reviewer states the RWD car turns in quickly and feels balanced, with no front-end push. Reviewer finds the steering light, with limited feedback. Reviewer saw efficiency fall from about 3.7 to 3.1 mi/kWh over 420 miles of mixed driving (about 292 miles of real range vs 370 EPA) and says the Lucid Air is far more efficient. Reviewer finds the dashboard screen design generic. Reviewer criticizes combining the driver-door buttons into a single panel as blatant cost-cutting. Reviewer calls the build quality top-shelf, with a solid feel and doors that shut with a reassuring thunk. Reviewer expects the piano-black plastic trim to scratch and age poorly. Reviewer states the hatchback makes loading large items easier and gives more space, especially with the rear seats folded. Reviewer notes the car costs about as much as a base Lucid Air and more than a Cadillac Lyriq (tested at $75,240). Reviewer values Audi's dealer network and its software maturity compared with EV start-ups.
